## Beginner’s Sourdough Bread Method

### 1. Levain – 8:00 a.m.

| Weight | Ingredient | Baker’s Percentage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 38g | Ripe sourdough starter (100% hydration) | 50.0% |
| 38g | Bob’s Red Mill Stoneground Whole Wheat | 50.0% |
| 38g | Bob’s Red Mill Artisan Bread Flour | 50.0% |
| 76g | Water | 100.0% |

Levain ingredients

Remember: the [*levain* is an off-shoot](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/what-is-a-levain-and-how-is-it-different-from-a-starter/) of your continually maintained sourdough starter and is likewise composed of bacteria and yeasts. You make this levain well before you mix the dough, so it has time to ferment, and eventually, it’s added to the dough to seed fermentation.

Mix the ingredients in the table above in a clean jar (I use the same [sourdough starter jars](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/the-best-jar-for-your-sourdough-starter/)) and leave it at warm room temperature, 74-76°F (23-24°C), for 5 to 6 hours. When it’s ready, it will be expanded, bubbly on top, inside, and at the sides, and have a slightly sour aroma. The photo below shows my levain before it goes into my dough mix.

[![sourdough levain](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%201000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-11.jpg)

Ripe sourdough levain ready for mixing.

### 2. Autolyse – 12:00 p.m.

| Weight | Ingredient |
| --- | --- |
| 773g | Bob’s Red Mill Artisan Bread Flour |
| 114g | Bob’s Red Mill Stoneground Whole Wheat Flour |
| 51g | Bob’s Red Mill Dark Rye Flour |
| 603g | Water (this has 50g less than the overall formula, reserved for Mix step below) |

Autolyse dough mix

The [desired dough temperature (DDT)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/the-importance-of-dough-temperature-in-baking/) for this dough is **78°F (25°C).** As described in the temperature section above, we will try to get the dough to this temperature right at the end of [mixing](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/mixing-bread-dough/) (which is also at the beginning of bulk fermentation).

Warm or cool the autolyse water so the mixed dough reaches the FDT for this recipe. Place the **flour** and the **water** called for in the table above in a large bowl. Use wet hands to mix until no dry bits remain; the dough will be shaggy and loose. Use a bowl scraper to scrape down the sides of the bowl, keeping all the dough in one area at the bottom. [Cover the bowl](https://amzn.to/2taFVyW) and place it near your levain for 1 hour.

[![hand mixing flour and water](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%201000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-13.jpg)

Mixing dough by hand.

Note that the autolyse stage does not incorporate salt or the levain in any way since the autolyse is a long one hour. Adding the levain to the autolyse would mean fermentation would begin, which could end up overproofing the dough. Salt is rarely added to an autolyse because the salt would diminish enzymatic activity during this time, which is precisely why we are doing an autolyse. The autolyse and levain are two separate entities that will be mixed together later in the process.

### 3. Mix – 1:00 p.m.

[![hand mixing levain, salt, flour and water](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%201000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-12.jpg)

Mixing Beginner’s Sourdough ingredients in by hand.

| Weight | Ingredient |
| --- | --- |
| 50g | Reserved water (this water was held back in the Autolyse step) |
| 18g | Fine sea salt |
| 190g | Ripe, 100% hydration levain (from Levain, above) |

Final dough mix ingredients

Use your instant-read thermometer to take the dough’s temperature and compare it to the FDT for this recipe. If it is higher, use cold water for the reserved water; if it is lower, use warm water.

At this point, your autolyse is complete and your levain is ready—it’s time to [mix and strengthen the dough](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/mixing-bread-dough/). If the dough feels very wet and shaggy, do not use all of the reserved 50g of water; use only a splash to help incorporate the salt and levain. If the dough feels good to you, use all the reserved water.

To the autolyse, add the ingredients in the table above (**salt**, reserved **water** to help [adjust dough hydration and consistency](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/dough-hydration/), and **levain**). I like to spread everything on top of the dough and use wet hands to pinch all the ingredients together. Transfer the dough to a container or thick-walled bowl for bulk fermentation.

Take the temperature of the dough to get your final dough temperature. If your FDT is below 78°F (25°C), next time use warmer water, and conversely, if it’s above 78°F (25°C), use cooler water. Cover the dough.

### 4. Bulk Fermentation – 1:10 p.m. to 5:10 p.m.

At 74-76°F (23-24°C) ambient temperature, bulk fermentation should go for about 4 hours. Perform 3 [sets of stretches and folds](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/how-to-stretch-and-fold-sourdough/) during bulk fermentation, spaced out by 30 minutes.

[![Beginner's Sourdough Bread via @theperfectloaf](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201080%201350'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-1-1.jpg)

Giving the dough a set of stretch and folds during bulk fermentation

Each set of stretches and folds consists of 4 folds: one each at the North, South, East, and West sides. Wet your hands with a little water to prevent sticking, and then lift one side (North) of the dough with two hands. Stretch the dough high enough so you can fold it completely over to the other side. Rotate the bowl 180° and do the other side (South). Finish the other two sides (East and West) to complete the set. Let the dough rest for 30 minutes, covered, between sets.

In the video below, you can see how I stretch and fold this dough during bulk fermentation.

After the third set of stretch and folds, let the dough rest for the remainder of bulk fermentation. During this time, fermentation aerates the dough (making it rise), continues to strengthen it, and further develops its flavor.

[![end of bulk fermentation](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%20834'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-2.jpg)

Beginner’s Sourdough Bread dough at the end of bulk fermentation

At the end of bulk fermentation, your dough should have risen by 20% to 50%. It should show some bubbles on the top and sides, and the edge of the dough where it meets the bowl should be slightly domed, which indicates strength. In the photo above, you can see all these signs. If you don’t see these signs, leave it for another 15 minutes in bulk fermentation and check again.

### 5. Divide and preshape – 5:15 p.m.

[![preshape](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%201000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-14.jpg)

Dividing and preshaping dough

Lightly flour a work surface. Using a bowl scraper, gently scrape the dough onto the work surface and use your bench knife to divide the dough directly in half. Using your bench knife in your dominant hand, and the other hand wet (or floured, if you prefer) to reduce sticking, turn each half of the dough on the counter while lightly pulling the dough towards you. This gentle turning and pulling motion will develop tension on the dough’s top, forming a circle.

Preshaping bread dough is an often overlooked step, but it sets the stage for successful shaping later. See my [guide to preshaping bread dough](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/how-to-preshape-bread-dough/) for more information.

Let the dough rest for 25 minutes, uncovered.

In the video below, you can see how I preshape this beginner’s sourdough bread dough:

### 6. Shape – 5:35 p.m.

[![shaping boules](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%20834'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-4.jpg)

If you’re new to shaping bread dough, check out my guide to [shaping a boule (a round)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) in addition to the steps below.

Lightly flour the top of your dough rounds and the work surface. Working with one round at a time, flip the round so the floured top is now down on the floured work surface.

As seen in the image below, with lightly floured hands, grab the bottom of the round and stretch it lightly downward towards your body, and then up and over about 2/3 of the way to the top.

Then, grab the left and right sides of the dough and stretch them away from each other. Fold one side over toward the other and repeat with the other side.

Then, grab the top of the circle, stretch it away from your body, and then fold it down to the bottom of the dough. You’ll now have a tight package that resembles a letter.

Finally, flip or roll down the dough so the seams are all on the bottom. Using both hands, cup the top part of the round and drag the dough gently towards your body to create surface tension on the dough. The angle of your hands will gently press the dough’s bottom on the counter. This dragging helps create surface tension on the dough, which helps keep it in shape during proofing.

[![shaping beginner's sourdough bread dough](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%201000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-15-1.jpg)

Shaping Beginner’s Sourdough Bread

Let the dough rest on the bench for a few minutes to help the bottom seam seal.

In the video below, you can see how I shape bread dough into a boule shape.

Meanwhile, prepare your proofing baskets. Line two proofing baskets, kitchen bowls, or bannetons with clean kitchen towels. Dust lightly and evenly with plain white flour or [white rice flour](https://amzn.to/2FNsHLi). Gently transfer each piece of shaped dough to a proofing basket, seam-side-up.

You can also top this dough with sesame seeds, sunflower seeds, pepitas, and much more—see my [guide to topping bread dough](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-top-bread-dough/) for more ideas and instructions.

### 7. Rest and proof – 5:40 p.m. to 9:30 a.m. (next day)

[![Beginner's Sourdough Bread via @theperfectloaf](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201080%201350'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-1-3.jpg)

To prevent your dough from drying out overnight, place your bowls containing your shaped dough into [reusable plastic bags](https://amzn.to/2RRnybO) and seal. I usually puff up the plastic bag around the bowl by opening it wide and then quickly closing it.

Let the dough rest on the counter for 20 minutes. Then, [retard](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/) (a baker’s term meaning place into a cold area to proof) in the refrigerator at 38°F (3°C) for 16 hours (overnight).

During this time, overall fermentation will slow (especially yeast activity), but bacterial activity will continue at a reduced rate, resulting in a more complex flavor and, ultimately, deeper crust coloring.

### 8. Bake – Next morning: preheat oven at 8:30 a.m., bake at 9:30 a.m.

Now, it’s time to bake your sourdough bread. It’s not a difficult step, but there are some things to know. The oven needs steam for the best crust and tallest rise. I like to use a Dutch oven or combo cooker, [which is very easy](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/cookbooks/videos/baking-bread-in-a-dutch-oven/). These pots trap the steam released from the dough and provide the right environment for it to rise optimally.

[![beginner's sourdough bread fully proofed](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%20834'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-5.jpg)

See [my full guide to baking sourdough bread](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/the-ultimate-guide-to-baking-bread-dough/) for tips on scoring your dough, pots, and steaming.

Place an oven rack in the bottom third of the oven with no rack above it. Put your combo cooker or Dutch oven on the oven rack, and preheat the oven to 450°F (232°C) for at least 30 minutes. If you’re using a combo cooker, place the shallow side face up on one side and the heavier, deep side face down on the other.

[![Beginner's Sourdough Bread via @theperfectloaf](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201080%201350'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-1-2.jpg)

When your oven is preheated, remove one of the proofing baskets from the fridge, uncover it, and place a piece of parchment paper over it. Place a pizza peel, cutting board, or inverted baking sheet on top of the parchment and, using both hands, flip everything over. Gently remove the basket; your dough should rest on the parchment.

Using a razor blade, sharp knife, or baker’s lame, score the dough at a 90° angle between the blade and the dough. I chose to make a “box” pattern. If using scissors, snip the dough a few times at a very shallow angle between the scissors and the dough, forming a set of ridges down the dough’s center.

[![scoring my beginner's sourdough bread](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201250%201000'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf-beginners-sourdough-bread-16.jpg)

Baking bread in a Dutch oven

While wearing your [heavy-duty oven mitt](https://amzn.to/3iD4MR4), and with caution, pull out your shallow side of the combo cooker and place it on a heat-safe rack or stovetop. Slide the dough into the combo cooker or Dutch oven. Place it back into the oven and cover the shallow side with the deep side, or put the lid on the Dutch oven. This sealed environment helps trap the moisture (escaping steam) from your dough to steam the loaf exterior as it bakes, which encourages maximal rise and a crunchy, shiny crust.

Bake for 20 minutes. Vent the oven of steam: use your oven mitt to very carefully remove the top of the combo cooker or Dutch oven. Leave the large side of the combo cooker in the oven to the side. Close the oven door and bake for 30 minutes more. When done, the loaf should have an internal temperature of around 208°F (97°C), and the crust should be a deep mahogany color and crackle/crunch when squeezed.

Use your oven mitt to transfer the bread to a wire rack carefully. Cool for 1 to 2 hours before slicing into your beginner’s sourdough bread. For the second loaf, preheat the combo cooker or Dutch oven for 15 minutes and repeat.

[Follow my guide to storing bread](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/the-best-way-to-store-bread/) to keep your loaves fresh for as long as possible.

[![Beginner's Sourdough Bread Crust](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201920%201281'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/theperfectloaf_beginners_sourdough_bread.jpg)

Baked Beginner’s Sourdough Bread with a deeply-colored and crunchy crust.

Once you get the hang of this beginner’s sourdough bread process and formula, you can endlessly modify it with add-ins like walnuts, cranberries, seeds, and a host of other ingredients bound only by your imagination. But the most important thing is to bake and have fun. Remember that sometimes bread doesn’t come out as you intended–but stick with it, and you’ll be rewarded time and time again.

And of course, buon appetito!

### Instructions

1. **Levain** (8:00 a.m.)  
   In a small container, mix the levain ingredients and keep at 74-76°F (23-24°C) for 5 to 6 hours.
2. **Autolyse** (12:00 p.m)  
   In a medium mixing bowl, mix the flour and 603 grams of water (reserve 50 grams until the next step). Cover and let rest for 1 hour.
3. **Mix** (1:00 p.m.)  
   To the mixing bowl holding your dough, add the salt, ripe levain (from step 1), and reserved 50 grams water. Mix by hand or with a dough whisk until incorporated. Transfer your dough to a bulk fermentation container and cover.
4. **Bulk Fermentation** (1:10 p.m. to 5:10 p.m.)  
   Give the dough 3 sets of stretch and folds at 30-minute intervals, where the first set starts 30 minutes after the start of bulk fermentation.
5. **Divide and Preshape** (5:10 p.m.)  
   Lightly flour your work surface and scrape out your dough. Using your bench knife, divide the dough in half. Lightly shape each half into a round shape. Let the dough rest for 25 minutes, uncovered.
6. **Shape** (5:35 p.m.)  
   Shape the dough into a round (boule) or oval (batard)—place in proofing baskets.
7. **Rest and Proof** (5:40 p.m. to 9:30 a.m. the next day)  
   Cover proofing baskets with reusable plastic and seal shut. Let the dough sit out on the counter for 20 minutes. Then, place both baskets into the refrigerator and proof overnight.
8. **Bake** (Preheat oven at 8:30 a.m., bake at 9:30 a.m.)  
   Preheat your oven with a combo cooker or Dutch oven inside to 450°F (230°C). When the oven is preheated, remove your dough from the fridge, score it, and transfer to the preheated combo cooker. Place the cooker in the oven, cover with the lid, and bake for 20 minutes. After this time, remove the lid (you can keep it in the oven or remove it) and continue to bake for 30 minutes longer. When done, the internal temperature should be around 208°F (97°C). Let the loaves cool for 1 to 2 hours on a wire rack before slicing.

### Notes

While the recipe calls for 16 hours of total proof time, you could extend this time and bake the loaves in the morning, afternoon, or even the evening on day two. Leave the proofing dough in the fridge until ready to bake.

## Beginner’s Sourdough Bread Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is sourdough bread good for you?

Sourdough, and its lengthy natural fermentation process, can help break down the gluten in grain, which helps aid in the body’s digestion. Additionally, fermentation helps “unlock” the nutrition inherent in the grain, allowing for better absorption.

### Is sourdough bread sour?

Sourdough isn’t super sour in the traditional sense—it’s not sour like taking a bit of a lemon. But it does have tanginess which is the byproduct of lactic acid fermentation. Sourdough bread will have more sourness than one made with 100% commercial yeast due to the acids created by natural fermentation.

### How can I make sourdough bread more sour?

To increase the sour flavor of this sourdough bread, add more whole grains (both to your sourdough starter and the dough itself), keep the dough warm (78°F/25°C or warmer), and lengthen the total fermentation time by keeping the dough in the fridge to proof even longer than the 16 hours specified in the recipe—24 hours is a good starting point.

### How can I get a more open crumb with my bread?

First, focus on your sourdough starter to get a more open crumb for this sourdough bread: it should be refreshed (fed) often, kept warm, and used when ripe. Next, strengthen the dough sufficiently during mixing and bulk fermentation by using stretches and folds. Finally, your dough must be fully proofed so that when you press a finger into the dough, it slowly springs back about halfway (if it springs back quickly, let it proof longer; if the finger indentation stays, bake immediately).

# How To Create A Sourdough Baking Schedule

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/e48ce1c56efdb224c092cf6b19ed130c45d254df0579fbc7a270432f3875f5d8?s=56&d=mm&r=g)

Learn how to create a sourdough baking schedule that fits your life, not the other way around. Flexible timelines, fermentation tips, and more.

![Sourdough baking schedule - Pinterest Image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='150'%20height='150'%20viewBox='0%200%20150%20150'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

One of the biggest misconceptions about sourdough bread is that it requires a rigid schedule. Or even worse, that you can’t bake sourdough bread if you have a busy life. The truth is, you can literally make sourdough work on any schedule. You just need to work with your schedule, not against it! I’m going to show you how to do this.

Making sourdough bread can be a lengthy process, but it can also be manipulated so that you can work the process around your life. You’re the boss here, not your sourdough starter! Whether you work full time or shift work, you’re a busy parent or you just enjoy not having to be a ruled by your dough, a sourdough baking schedule means you can bake sourdough on your terms.

![Two bannetons of sourdough sitting next to a coffee machine. There are a pair of hands in the photo and one hand is picking up a banneton and the other hand is picking up a green coffee mug filled with coffee. ](https://pantrymama.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/BAKE-SOURDOUGH-IN-THE-MORNING-HORIZONTAL-IMAGE.jpg)

This post contains affiliate links. Please see our [disclosure policy](https://pantrymama.com/affiliate-disclosure/).

## Table of Contents

## What Is a Sourdough Bread Timeline?

A sourdough bread timeline is simply a roadmap that shows the major stages of making sourdough bread from start to finish.

Most sourdough loaves follow the same basic process:

![An infographic outlining the 9 stages of baking sourdough bread.](https://pantrymama.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/STAGES-OF-MAKING-SOURDOUGH-BREAD.jpg)

The challenge is that every one of these stages can vary depending on your starter, your dough temperature, your kitchen environment, and the type of bread you’re making. That’s why copying someone else’s sourdough schedule doesn’t always work.

Instead of focusing on exact times, successful sourdough bakers learn to understand what is happening during each stage so they can make adjustments when life inevitably gets in the way. They understand how to use [baker’s percentages](https://pantrymama.com/understanding-bakers-math/), [sourdough starter ratios](https://pantrymama.com/sourdough-starter-ratios/) and [temperature adjustments](https://pantrymama.com/making-sourdough-in-hotter-or-colder-temperatures/) to create flexibility in their baking.

![Kate from The Pantry Mama stirring a jar of sourdough starter while wearing a blue t-shirt.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1800'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201800'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Weekday Sourdough Baking Schedule

Here is an example of a baking timeline that you could use to fit sourdough into your life (it’s the one I use to bake sourdough for my busy family). It’s based on my [Simple Sourdough Bread recipe](https://pantrymama.com/how-to-bake-simple-sourdough-bread/) which uses a [fermentolyse](https://pantrymama.com/autolyse-vs-fermentolyse/) rather than autolyse. I also use high protein bread flour to create a stretchy and elastic dough.

**DAY 1**  
1.00 pm – Feed sourdough starter 1:1:1 ratio.  
5.00 pm – Premix and Fermentolyse with 50 grams of active starter (while I cook dinner).  
6.30 pm – Form into a smooth ball. Rest for 30 minutes.  
7.00 pm – Perform 4-6 sets of stretch & folds over next 2 hours to develop the gluten network.  
9.00 pm – Cover and leave on kitchen counter overnight at room temp for bulk ferment.

![A glass bowl of sourdough sitting in front of a wooden chopping board where orange carrots and green peppers are being chopped up and put into a turquoise colored Dutch oven to the right of the photo.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='800'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20800'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

**DAY 2**  
6.00 am – The next morning, shape & lift your bread dough into a banneton/bowl, cover with a plastic bag or elastic food cover & place into the fridge.  
*(I could bake my bread from around 2pm today if I wanted to, I just prefer a longer cold ferment).*

**DAY 3**  
2.00pm – Score the top of the dough and place into hot Dutch oven using a piece of parchment paper.  
7.00pm – Cut into delicious sourdough to serve with dinner.

![A vertical image of a planner open to a page showing a few appointments. There is a also a cambro container filled with sourdough dough. In the background of the photo, you can see a green coffee mug, chocolate chip cookie and a bowl of dough.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1800'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201800'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Why Most Sourdough Schedules Fail

Most sourdough baking schedules fail because they focus too heavily on the clock. Sourdough fermentation is a biological process driven by wild yeast and bacteria. These microorganisms don’t know what time it is, and they certainly don’t care what a recipe says. A dough that takes 4 hours to bulk ferment in a warm kitchen might take 10 hours in a cool kitchen.

The [strength of your starter](https://pantrymama.com/5-ways-to-strengthen-a-sourdough-starter-give-your-starter-a-boost/), the flour you’re using, the amount of starter in the dough, and even the temperature of your water can all dramatically affect how quickly fermentation progresses. This is why I always say watch your dough and not the clock! Learning to recognize the [signs of proper bulk fermentation](https://pantrymama.com/bulk-fermentation-finished/) will always be more valuable than memorizing a timeline.

## How Can You Take Charge of Your Sourdough Baking Schedule?

Things like feeding ratios, [starter amounts](https://pantrymama.com/sourdough-starter-amount-matters/), temperature controls and your fridge will become crucial elements to allowing this to happen. The truth is that sourdough is far more flexible than most people realize. There are just lots of people out there that like to [over complicate sourdough](https://pantrymama.com/5-signs-youre-over-complicating-sourdough/). Once you understand the stages of fermentation and what your dough is actually doing, you can build a sourdough baking schedule that works around your life, not the other way around.

As someone who has helped thousands of home bakers across the globe learn sourdough, I’ve discovered that the most successful bakers aren’t the ones with the most time. They’re the ones who understand how to adapt the process to fit their schedule. You don’t need more time to bake sourdough, you just need to understand how to fit the process around your life.

Whether you’re working full-time, raising young children, managing shift work, or simply trying to squeeze baking into a busy week, this guide will help you create a sourdough timeline that works for you. If you are a busy mom, you might like these [sourdough secrets for busy moms](https://pantrymama.com/sourdough-secrets-for-busy-moms/).

## Create Your Own Sourdough Baking Schedule

The best sourdough schedule is the one that works for your life.

Ask yourself:

![A jar of sourdough starter that has just been fed sitting next to a green coffee mug. There is a kettle being boiled to the left of the coffee mug.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='800'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20800'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Once you understand the stages of fermentation, you can begin [adjusting starter amounts in your dough](https://pantrymama.com/sourdough-starter-amount-matters/), temperatures, and [cold proofing times](https://pantrymama.com/proofing-sourdough-in-the-fridge/) to build a schedule that feels natural. That’s when sourdough becomes enjoyable instead of overwhelming. You can make incredible sourdough bread, no matter what life throws at you!

You can learn how to mix the dough when you get home from work, stretch and fold before going to bed and then shape the dough the next day before going to work. You can then bake your sourdough at a specific time later in the day.

After helping millions of people bake sourdough, I’ve learned that success isn’t about finding the perfect timeline. It’s about understanding fermentation well enough to adapt the process to your life.

Whether you’re baking around work, school runs, sports practice, vacations, or busy family schedules, sourdough can absolutely work for you. You don’t need to fit your life around sourdough. You just need a sourdough timeline that fits your life.

![Sourdough baking schedule - Pinterest Image](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1000'%20height='1500'%20viewBox='0%200%201000%201500'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Frequently Asked Questions

While a typical sourdough loaf can take anywhere from 12 to 36 hours from feeding your starter to baking the bread, most of that time is hands-off fermentation. The exact timeline depends on your starter strength, dough temperature, and whether you choose to cold ferment your dough in the refrigerator. Understanding fermentation allows you to adjust the schedule to fit your life rather than following a rigid timeline.

Many home bakers use overnight fermentation to fit sourdough around work and family commitments. The key is understanding how temperature affects fermentation so your dough doesn’t overproof. It’s literally making sourdough while you sleep.

The easiest way to make sourdough fit your schedule is to use the refrigerator as a scheduling tool. Adjusting your starter feeding ratio, dough temperature, and fermentation times can also help speed up or slow down the process. Rather than following a fixed schedule, focus on understanding the stages of fermentation and adapting them to your daily routine.

A slightly longer fermentation is often not a problem and can even make your sourdough taste more sour. If life gets busy, placing the dough in the refrigerator can help slow fermentation and give you more flexibility. However, excessively long fermentation can lead to over proofing, which may affect the loaf’s structure, oven spring and flavor.

No! Sourdough fermentation needs to occur at room temp – particularly for the first part of the fermentation. The second part can be done in the fridge. You can read about how bulk fermentation differs from cold fermentation [here](https://pantrymama.com/bulk-ferment-vs-cold-ferment/).

The best sourdough baking schedule is the one that works for your lifestyle. Many busy bakers feed their starter in the evening, mix dough before bed, allow it to bulk ferment overnight, shape it in the morning, and bake the following day. Using cold fermentation gives you the flexibility to bake when it’s convenient rather than when the dough demands it.

No. Sourdough recipes provide estimated timelines, but fermentation is influenced by temperature, starter activity, flour choice, and hydration. The most successful sourdough bakers learn to read their dough rather than relying solely on the clock. Once you understand what properly fermented dough looks like, you can confidently adapt almost any sourdough baking routine to fit your life

# Understanding Sourdough Hydration

**AFFILIATE NOTIFICATION:**

![Sourdough Hydration Explained](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/sourdough-hydration-guide-683x1024.jpg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 1")
![Sourdough Hydration Explained](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/sourdough-hydration-guide-683x1024.jpg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 1")

Sourdough hydration is one of the most confusing concepts in sourdough baking—especially for U.S. home bakers used to measuring by cups and following exact timelines.

If you’ve ever wondered why your dough feels sticky, looks different than recipe photos, or behaves unpredictably even when you follow instructions, hydration is usually the reason.

This guide explains **what sourdough hydration actually means**, how it affects dough over time, and why long cold-rise sourdough often feels wetter than expected—**without turning this into a math lesson**. Use the table of contents to explore specific topics, or read straight through for a complete understanding of sourdough hydration.

![Side-by-side sourdough crumb comparison showing structural difference](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Side-By-Side-Hydration-differences-1024x819.jpg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 2")
![Side-by-side sourdough crumb comparison showing structural difference](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20819'%3E%3Crect%20width='1024'%20height='819'%20style='fill:%23e3e3e3'/%3E%3C/svg%3E "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 2")

## What Does “Hydration” Mean in Sourdough?

In sourdough baking, hydration refers to the **ratio of water to flour by weight** in a dough.

Hydration affects [dough structure](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/what-is-dough-structure-in-sourdough/) and feel, [fermentation speed](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/how-to-proof-sourdough-bread/), [crumb structure](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/how-to-control-sourdough-crumb/), and [oven spring](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/how-to-shape-sourdough-bread/). It does **not** determine whether a recipe is good or bad.

Because sourdough relies on long fermentation instead of kneading, sourdough hydration tends to be higher than in most yeast breads. This is normal—and intentional.

![Window Pane Test-last stretch and fold](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/IMG_0625-1.jpg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 3")
![Window Pane Test-last stretch and fold](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/IMG_0625-1.jpg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 3")

## Why Sourdough Dough Often Feels Wetter Than Expected

Sourdough recipes — especially artisan loaves — use **higher hydration** than typical yeast breads. This is intentional. Many artisan sourdough recipes use higher sourdough hydration because water supports long fermentation and dough building:

As a result, sourdough dough often feels sticky early on, slack during bulk fermentation, and stronger later than expected. This surprises many bakers, but it’s normal—especially in [long cold-rise methods](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/cold-proof-vs-cold-bulk-sourdough/).

***Our [Sourdough Troubleshooting Guide](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/sourdough-troubleshooting-guide/)*** ***walks through how hydration, fermentation timing, gluten development, and flour choice interact so you can identify the actual cause of your problem if you are not happy with your sourdough.***

## Hydration Is a Range — Not a Rule

Hydration is **not a fixed number that works for everyone**. The same hydration can behave very differently depending on:

![autolyse stage- sourdough hydration](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/autolyse-stage-sourdough-bread.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 4")
![autolyse stage- sourdough hydration](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/autolyse-stage-sourdough-bread.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 4")

This is why two bakers can follow the same recipe and get a different dough. The more water you try to force into the your flour, the more it changes the processes need to accommodate that extra moisture. You need a high protein flour to increase hydration significantly.

![85% hydration dough. Very loose structure at 1st stretch. cannot coil yet. ](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/ist-stretch-and-fold.jpeg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 5")
![85% hydration dough. Very loose structure at 1st stretch. cannot coil yet. ](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/ist-stretch-and-fold.jpeg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 5")

### Advanced Perspective: Sourdough Hydration Is a Lever, Not a Target

For experienced bakers, hydration is best understood as a *lever* rather than a fixed percentage. Changing hydration alters how fermentation expresses itself, how gluten develops, and how dough responds to time and temperature.

Higher hydration amplifies flour differences, fermentation speed, and handling errors. This means it’s trickier to work with high hydration doughs. Lower hydration dough is much easier to handle and increases beginner success.

Mastery comes from choosing hydration intentionally based on flour choice, fermentation method, and desired crumb structure. Our table further down this post will help with that.

### Using a Real Recipe to Understand Sourdough Hydration (Math vs. Behavior)

Our [Beginner Sourdough Artisan Bread](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/tartine-style-sourdough-bread-recipe/) is at 78% hydration. This is high for a beginner loaf. However,   
It works exceptionally well for beginners because the **process is designed to support that hydration**. **Here’s How it works:**

The result is a dough that behaves more like a moderate-hydration dough—elastic, resilient, and predictable—despite its higher hydration number. This is why hydration should be evaluated not just by the numbers, but by how the dough is developed, fermented, and handled.

![beginner sourdough artisan bread](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/IMG_4955.jpeg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 6")
![beginner sourdough artisan bread](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/IMG_4955.jpeg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 6")

This recipe is a good example of why the hydration table below focuses on **dough behavior**, not just percentages.

## Sourdough Hydration Comparison: Low vs. Medium vs. High

Hydration is not an isolated knob. Changing water alone affects **gluten strength, fermentation speed, crumb texture, loaf shape, and flavor**. The comparison section below is designed to help you predict those changes, at a glance, *before* you mix the dough—so hydration becomes a tool, not a surprise.

## Low Hydration Sourdough (60–65%)

## Medium Hydration Sourdough (66–72%)

![well risen sourdough bread with open crumb showing ideal fermentation and oven spring](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/why-is-my-sourdough-bread-dense-open-crumb-example.jpg-.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 7")
![well risen sourdough bread with open crumb showing ideal fermentation and oven spring](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/why-is-my-sourdough-bread-dense-open-crumb-example.jpg-.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 7")

## High Hydration Sourdough (73–85%+)

![High Hydration Beginner Artisan Bread 85](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/High-Hydration-Beginner-Artisan-Bread-85.jpeg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 8")
![High Hydration Beginner Artisan Bread 85](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/High-Hydration-Beginner-Artisan-Bread-85.jpeg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 8")

***Hydration should be chosen intentionally based on flour strength, fermentation method, and your skill level — not simply pushed higher for open crumb.***

## How to Use This Section Intentionally

To use the comparison section, first decide **what you want to change**, then adjust hydration intentionally for the results you are going for.

**Remember:**

![Side-by-side crumb comparison of two sourdough loaves showing structure difference between properly measured moderate hydration and higher hydration dough](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/diferent-bakes-and-hydration-same-recipe-1024x623.jpeg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 9")
![Side-by-side crumb comparison of two sourdough loaves showing structure difference between properly measured moderate hydration and higher hydration dough](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/diferent-bakes-and-hydration-same-recipe-1024x623.jpeg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 9")

## Real-Life Hydration Test: What Happens When Water Increases Without Process Adjustment

Recently, I baked the same sourdough recipe twice using identical flour, starter strength, salt, and fermentation timing. The only variable that changed was hydration. These are the pictures you see in this post for the finished bakes.

One loaf was measured carefully at the intended hydration level. The other loaf was mixed more casually, with slightly more water added and less precise flour measurement. It probably raised hydration to 79 or 80% due to sloppy measurements.

Here is what happened:

The properly measured loaf:

The key takeaway was not that higher hydration “fails.”  
The takeaway was that hydration changes must be paired with adjustments in gluten development,(learn more about [Sourdough Flour Types here](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/sourdough-flour-types-guide/)) shaping precision, and fermentation control.

When water increases but process stays the same, structure weakens.

This side-by-side bake reinforced an important principle:

**Hydration should be adjusted intentionally—not accidentally.**

Exact measurement and disciplined process produce consistent results. Casual adjustments produce unpredictable structure.

![Side-by-side sourdough crumb comparison showing structural difference between two hydration levels using the same recipe and process](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Side-By-Side-Hydration-differences-1024x819.jpg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 10")
![Side-by-side sourdough crumb comparison showing structural difference between two hydration levels using the same recipe and process](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Side-By-Side-Hydration-differences-1024x819.jpg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 10")

### Salt & Hydration (Important Note)

Salt does **not** change dough hydration on paper, but it **changes how hydrated the dough behaves**.

**Takeaway:**  
***A dough may feel “too wet” before salt is added, then suddenly manageable afterward. Always evaluate hydration after salt incorporation, not before.***

### Hydration Adjustment Checklist

**Before increasing hydration, confirm the following:**

☐ Flour has sufficient protein (bread flour preferred)  
☐ Starter is recently fed, active, and predictable  
☐ Autolyse is complete before salt is added  
☐ Gluten development includes multiple stretch-and-folds  
☐ Bulk fermentation is monitored by *rise percentage*, not time  
☐ Shaping technique builds surface tension  
☐ Baking method provides strong steam (Dutch oven)

**If more than two boxes are unchecked, do not increase hydration yet.**

### NOTE: Don’t Increase Hydration Unless You Also…

**Higher hydration magnifies mistakes. Structure must increase with water**

![Sourdough Whole Wheat Artisan Bread has moderate sourdough hydration. ](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/cropped-Sourdough-Whole-Wheat-Artisan-Bread.jpg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 11")
![Sourdough Whole Wheat Artisan Bread has moderate sourdough hydration. ](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/cropped-Sourdough-Whole-Wheat-Artisan-Bread.jpg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 11")

## How Flour Choice Affects Hydration

Different flours and add in ingredients like oatmeal, absorb water differently. Strong bread flour can support higher hydration, while all-purpose or whole wheat flour may behave very differently. For a deeper breakdown of protein levels, structure strength, and flour performance in sourdough, [read our complete guide to choosing the right flour for sourdough bread](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/sourdough-flour-types-guide/).

Hydration and flour must always be balanced together. Our [sourdough oatmeal bread](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/oatmeal-bread-no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe/) is an example of a mathematically very high hydration bread of over 100% hydration. However, since the oatmeal is par cooked in some water it traps some hydration and creates a very workable dough.

*This is why we recommend strong flour (4–5g protein per serving) for long cold-rise sourdough.*

![Oval sourdough loaf crumb showing properly balanced hydration and fermentation](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/beginner-Artisan-Sourdough-Bread-961x1024.jpeg "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 12")
![Oval sourdough loaf crumb showing properly balanced hydration and fermentation](https://www.homemadefoodjunkie.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/beginner-Artisan-Sourdough-Bread-961x1024.jpeg.webp "Understanding Sourdough Hydration 12")

## Why Hydration Matters More in Long Cold-Rise Sourdough

In long fermentation, hydration compounds over time. Water continues to redistribute, starches break down, and gluten relaxes slowly in the refrigerator. Dough that feels manageable at mixing can feel much wetter, and lighter with lots of bubbles in it 12–24 hours later. This is a good thing.

Hydration choices that work for same-day doughs often fail in long cold-rise sourdough unless flour strength and fermentation are adjusted accordingly.

## What Sourdough Hydration Percentage Really Means

In sourdough baking, hydration refers to the **ratio of water to flour by weight**, expressed as a percentage. If a dough contains 500 grams of flour and 350 grams of water, the hydration level is 70%.

Hydration percentage matters because even small changes dramatically affect dough behavior. A 5% increase in hydration can turn an easy-to-handle dough into one that feels sticky, slack, or difficult to shape. Understanding hydration allows you to troubleshoot problems like dense crumb, flat loaves, and weak oven spring with intention instead of trial and error.

Hydration is also inseparable from flour type, fermentation time, and gluten development. There is no “one perfect hydration,” only the **right hydration for your flour, skill level, and environment**.

## Sourdough Hydration FAQs

### Is sticky sourdough dough normal?

Yes. Sticky dough is normal in sourdough, especially in higher hydration or long cold-rise recipes. Sourdough relies on time rather than kneading, so dough often starts sticky and gains strength gradually as gluten develops and fermentation progresses. Stickiness alone does not mean the dough is too wet or failed.

### Does higher hydration make better sourdough bread?

Not always. Higher hydration can create a more open crumb, but only when gluten development, flour strength, and fermentation are properly balanced. Without enough structure, higher hydration weakens dough, causing flat loaves, poor oven spring, or gummy crumb. Better bread comes from balance, not maximum water.

### Why does sourdough dough feel wetter after refrigeration?

During long cold fermentation, water continues to redistribute and gluten slowly relaxes. Dough that felt manageable at mixing often feels wetter after 12–24 hours in the refrigerator. This is normal for cold-rise sourdough and does not automatically mean hydration is too high.

### Should beginners use low hydration sourdough recipes?

Yes, most beginners succeed faster with low to moderate hydration sourdough. These doughs are easier to handle, more forgiving of timing errors, and better for learning fermentation cues. Higher hydration doughs are best attempted after developing confidence with shaping and fermentation control.

### Does salt change sourdough hydration?

Salt does not change hydration percentage, but it changes how hydrated the dough behaves. Salt tightens gluten, binds some free water, and slows fermentation, making dough feel firmer and easier to handle. Dough should always be evaluated after salt is added, not before.

### Why does my sourdough behave differently even when I follow the same recipe?

Sourdough behavior varies due to flour type, protein content, fermentation time, temperature, and measurement accuracy. Even small changes in these factors can alter hydration behavior. This is why sourdough recipes must be adjusted by feel and fermentation cues, not timing alone.

Sourdough hydration is not about chasing a number—it’s about understanding the relationship between **water, flour, fermentation, and technique**. When hydration is balanced with strong flour and proper fermentation, dough becomes predictable instead of frustrating. Once you understand that relationship, sourdough baking becomes consistent, flexible, and enjoyable.
